analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates at 36% for consumer, small business, and nonprofit loans during the COVID emergency.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one senator with a single cosponsor, the bill never received a markup or vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have extended protections that already apply to servicemembers under the Military Lending Act to everyone during the COVID-19 emergency: no loan to a consumer, small business, or charity could carry an annual interest rate above 36%. It also tightened how card fees and credit-insurance charges count toward that rate, kept stronger state laws in place, and let state attorneys general sue violators. The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee, got one hearing, and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers taking on debt during the pandemic — households using credit cards, small businesses borrowing to stay open, and charities — would have been shielded from the highest-cost emergency loans. Servicemembers already get this 36% cap; the bill would have given the same shield to everyone else, with state enforcers able to sue lenders who broke it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pandemic-era borrowers, small businesses, and charities

how_it_helps.text: Applies the Military Lending Act's protections — including its 36% annual rate cap — to all consumer credit, small business credit, and 501(c)(3) charities for loans made during the COVID-19 emergency [S2, S3].

Requires lenders to count charges like single-premium credit insurance and add-on ancillary products toward the rate calculation for credit cards, using the Defense Department's rules for servicemembers [S3].

Barred the consumer bureau from granting exemptions, kept stronger state rate caps in force, and gave state attorneys general and state regulators three years to sue violators and win the same remedies that apply under the Military Lending Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-rate consumer lenders and credit card issuers, whose interest and fee income on loans made during the emergency would have been capped. A good-faith objection: a hard 36% ceiling can make it unprofitable to lend to the riskiest borrowers, so some could have lost access to any formal emergency credit [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday, title, and credit card lenders

drawbacks.text: A 36% cap on all emergency-period credit [S2, S3] would make payday- and title-style lending unworkable, and lenders might simply stop serving subprime borrowers — the same tradeoff Congress weighed when it capped rates for the military.
The cap was temporary, covering only loans made during the COVID-19 emergency declaration, so it would not have addressed high-rate debt before or after the crisis [S3].

Federal and qualifying state credit unions were carved out [S3]; they already operate under a lower federal credit union rate limit, so the exemption is regulatory relief rather than a rate increase, but it does add a two-tier structure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: a hard ceiling on emergency-period loan costs for exactly the households and small businesses most likely to borrow desperately in a pandemic, with the military's proven enforcement machinery attached. The main cost is the classic one for any rate cap — some high-risk borrowers may find no lawful lender at all — but the cap applies only while the emergency lasts, which limits both the protection and that risk.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee never voted on it; it was referred there in March 2020, got one hearing in May, and stayed put until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Van Hollen introduced the bill on March 22, 2020, weeks into the COVID-19 national emergency, and it was read twice and referred to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S3, S5].
It had one cosponsor, Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio [S4].
The committee held a hearing on May 12, 2020, but the bill was never reported out, never came to a Senate vote, and received no further action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-rate consumer lenders and credit card issuers, which kept charging uncapped interest and fees on loans made during the pandemic; borrowers got no federal rate ceiling, and relief instead came through other vehicles such as forbearance provisions.

for.name: Chris Van Hollen
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MD), sponsor, member of the Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to the Banking Committee during the first weeks of the COVID emergency.

for.name: Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on May 12, 2020, the only action the bill received after referral.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it remained in committee through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Banking Committee never advanced the bill to a vote.

industries.industry: Payday, title, and high-rate installment lenders
industries.note: The bill would have capped every emergency-period loan at 36% APR, far below the triple-digit rates this industry charges, ending its core product for the duration. Lenders profit by charging desperate borrowers more, so their interest ran directly against the borrowers the bill protected.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer finance companies
industries.note: During the emergency the bill would have applied the military rate calculation, pulling credit insurance and add-on product fees into the APR, trimming interest and fee income on card lending. Those fees are typically borne by customers who can least afford them.

Credit unions were exempted from the new cap so long as they stayed under their existing federal credit union rate limit, sparing them compliance costs while higher-rate competitors were capped. Credit unions already operate under that lower cap, so their members' rates would not have changed.
